title: Advisory practices lacking in AI policy
full_text:
The latest research from adviser technology provider intelliflo has found only 44 per cent of practices using artificial intelligence (AI) are doing so with a formal policy and approved tools in place.
This is despite the fact the analysis revealed 81 per cent of firms are using this form of technology.
Further, the intelliflo inaugural “Australian Advice Efficiency Survey” showed the most common usage of AI was for file notes, followed by advice documentation generation and client engagement activities.
Intelliflo chief executive and co-founder Nick Eatock said the results indicated AI had entered the mainstream of financial advice, with advisers increasingly using it to support core advice functions, client engagement and documentation.
However, Eatock noted at many practices the speed of adoption is outpacing the development of governance frameworks.
“Advisers are understandably enthusiastic about the productivity gains AI can deliver, but they’re also telling us they want greater certainty around how these tools should be governed, monitored and applied within a regulated advice environment,” he explained.
From a governance perspective, the report confirmed 34 per cent of AI-using firms have informal guidelines only, 13 per cent leave it up to individual discretion and 9 per cent are developing a policy.
With regard to concerns about AI usage, the research found inaccurate or misleading outputs were the biggest concern at 42 per cent, followed by data security and privacy at 32 per cent.
The survey also asked advisers what their biggest constraint on growth was, with 46 per cent citing capacity, 15 per cent saying technology, 13 per cent indicating lead generation and 12 per cent nominating the recruitment or retention of staff.
“Technology alone won’t solve the capacity challenge, but it is one of the most powerful levers available to the profession,” Eatock noted.
“If we want advice to become more accessible, businesses need tools that reduce administrative burden, improve efficiency and allow advisers to spend more time doing what they do best – helping clients.”
The intelliflo “Australian Advice Efficiency Survey” canvassed 101 Australian financial advice professionals.
